layout.title: How electricity gets to your outlet

shows.does: a lamp stands by the house wall, a wire runs from it over a pylon back to the power plant
the long wire between the pylon and the pole shimmers with heat while the lamp stays dark
a big transformer appears by the power plant and the heat on the wire stops
a flash bursts at the lamp
a gray transformer can appears at the pole and its light comes on
a glowing outline traces the pole
rain pours and the wire from the pole to the house snaps and falls
a trench is dug, a cable runs underground from the pole to the house and is covered
water drips onto the buried cable in the ground and it sparks
a sealed white pipe grows around the cable and the sparks stop
smoke curls out of the wall by the outlet
a breaker box appears, its switch flips down and the smoke stops
the plug goes into the outlet and the lamp glows warm
the lamp glows while current pulses along the wires

layout.why: A house with your lamp by its wall, wired to a power plant across the lawn by a pylon and a utility pole; the story follows the power from the plant along the line to the pole, the house, the wall and the outlet. Each problem is seen on the thing itself (heat shimmer on the line, a flash at the lamp, a snapped wire in the storm, smoke out of the wall), each fix lands where the problem was, and it ends close on the lamp lighting up when it is plugged in.

sentences.text: If you wire a power plant to your lamp, you have electricity.
But the long wire turns power into heat.
So a transformer raises the voltage to keep it cool.
But that voltage would fry your lamp.
So a transformer by the pole steps it down.
But a storm snaps the wire off the pole.
So you dig and bury the cable.
But water seeps into the buried cable, and it sparks.
So you run the cable inside a sealed pipe.
But inside the wall, overloaded wires heat up.
So a breaker trips before the wire burns.
Plug in the lamp, and it lights up.
Congratulations, you have built the power grid.
